conversation.content:
Good morning! I’m so glad we’re getting a chance to sit down together. My name is Dr. Bennett, and I’m the perinatal-mental-health clinician here. I know these early weeks with a new baby can feel like a whirlwind, so thank you for making time for yourself today.

I’ll be using a short questionnaire called the EPDS to check in on how you’re feeling emotionally since giving birth. It’s simply a way to make sure we’re not missing anything that might be making motherhood harder than it needs to be. Everything you share is confidential, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever is true for you right now.

We’ll go through ten questions about the past seven days. I’ll ask each one conversationally; you can answer however feels most comfortable, and we’ll take it at your pace. If at any point you feel uneasy, we can pause.

Ready to begin? Here’s the first question:

Over the past week, when you think about the times you were able to laugh or see the funny side of things, how did that feel for you?

[twists the tissue in her lap, eyes on the floor]

I… I can still laugh, I guess, but it feels kind of distant—like I’m hearing myself from far away. My husband made a joke yesterday about the baby’s funny faces and I smiled, but it didn’t feel the same as before. Mostly I’m just too tired or worried to find things funny.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[shrugs slightly, voice quiet]

Most of the time I haven’t really felt like laughing. I can still chuckle if something’s genuinely funny, but it’s pretty rare—maybe once or twice in the past week. It just doesn’t come naturally right now.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[hesitates, fidgeting with the hem of her sweater]

There are a couple things I still look forward to—like when my sister brings coffee on Thursdays—but even those feel kind of muted. I used to get excited about little plans, and now it’s more like… I know I should enjoy them, but the spark isn’t really there. I’d say only sometimes.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[eyes well up, voice cracks]

Yeah… I do that a lot. Like, if the baby won’t settle, I immediately think it’s because I’m not doing something right or I’m not patient enough. Even when my husband says it’s normal, I keep replaying what I did wrong. It’s not constant, but it’s there most days.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[dabs at her eyes with the tissue]

Almost every day. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure she’s stopped breathing, even though she’s right there in my arms. Or I’ll lie awake picturing ridiculous things—like the stroller rolling into traffic. I know it’s unlikely, but I can’t shut the thoughts off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[breathing a little faster, hands clasped tight]

Yes… a few times. It’s like this sudden wave—my chest gets tight, I feel shaky, and I have to check the baby every few minutes to make sure she’s okay. There’s no real reason; it just hits out of nowhere and then lingers for a while.
Things have been getting on top of me

[voice drops, shoulders slump]

Most days, yeah. Between the feedings, the laundry, trying to sleep… it feels like I’m drowning in small stuff. Some moments I can talk myself through it, but a lot of the time I just think, “I can’t keep up,” and I want to hide in the bathroom for five minutes so no one needs anything from me.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[looks down, voice barely above a whisper]

That’s been happening. I finally get her down, crawl into bed myself, and then my mind just… spins. I replay every little thing I might’ve messed up, or I picture scary “what-ifs” about her safety. It takes me an hour or more to fall asleep, and I wake up a couple times in a panic.
I have felt sad or miserable

[swallows hard, eyes glassy]

Pretty much every day this week. It’s like there’s this gray cloud that follows me around. I’ll be changing her diaper or rocking her and just feel this heaviness settle in. Sometimes it lifts for a little while, but it always comes back.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[presses the crumpled tissue under her eyes]

Twice… maybe three times. Yesterday I put her in the car seat and the strap twisted—such a dumb little thing—and I just sat on the floor crying. It feels like the tears are right under the surface most of the time.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[glances away, voice almost inaudible]

Once or twice this week… just fleeting. Like I’ll be exhausted and think, “What if I just kept driving past the house and never came back?” or imagine not waking up. I don’t have a plan or anything, and I’d never leave my baby, but the thoughts pop in before I can stop them.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Post-partum Depression / Anxiety Risk Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Demographic: Postpartum mother, infant age not specified.

Symptom Endorsement  
- Anhedonia: marked reduction in ability to laugh/look forward to events; enjoyment “muted.”  
- Persistent low mood: “gray cloud,” daily sadness most of this week.  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame re infant care (“not doing something right”).  
- Daily, intrusive anxious worries (infant safety, catastrophes); panic episodes with chest tightness, shakiness, no clear trigger.  
- Overwhelm: “drowning in small stuff,” urges to hide.  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia linked to rumination and fear.  
- Crying spells 2–3× week, precipitated by minor frustrations.  
- Passive self-harm ideation twice this week (e.g., thought of not waking up, driving away); denies intent or plan.

Observed Signs  
- Tearfulness, pressured speech during anxiety items, fidgeting, avoids eye contact when discussing self-harm.

Pattern  
Symptoms cluster consistent with moderate-to-severe postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; functional impact evident (sleep, coping, enjoyment). Passive suicidal ideation present → elevated safety risk.

Screening Significance  
- Score suggests referral for comprehensive diagnostic evaluation and safety planning.  
- Consider Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) for quantification; current verbal endorsement of self-harm warrants immediate risk assessment (EPDS item 10 ≥ 1).  
- Monitor support system, infant care capacity, psychosocial stressors.

Risk Summary  
1. Passive suicidal thoughts (low frequency, no plan).  
2. Daily anxiety/panic; interference with sleep and functioning.  
3. Pronounced guilt / low self-worth.  
4. Emotional lability and overwhelm impairing maternal coping.

Recommendation (screening only)  
Urgent clinical interview to determine diagnosis, safety, and appropriate level of care; consider involving OB/GYN and psychiatric provider for expedited follow-up.
